Order 
This petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 has been filed by the petitioner challenging the order dated 30.11.2023 passed by the learned 8th Additional Sessions Judge, Gwalior in Criminal Revision No. 433/2023, whereby the criminal revision preferred by the petitioner was dismissed.

The said revision had been filed against the order dated 19.10.2023 passed by the learned trial Court, by which the application under Section 65 of the Indian Evidence Act,
1872 preferred by respondent/accused was allowed.

2. In brief, the facts of the case are that the complainant, Smt. Bhagwati Sahu, submitted a complaint before the Trial Court against the accused, stating that in December 2013 the accused came along with the complainant's son Sonu and represented that he was a contractor of Canara NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:7860 2 MCRC-406-2024 Bank and was engaged in the installation of ATMs for the said bank.
He further stated that an ATM was to be installed at Naka Chandrabadni and that if the complainant rented out her shop for the said purpose, she would receive a monthly rent of Rs.15,000/-.
For this purpose, the complainant was required to construct a partition wall in the middle of her shop and to pay Rs.20,000/- towards bank formalities and processing charges.

Relying upon the representation of the accused, the complainant paid Bhagwati Sahu W/O Shri Sundar Lal Sahu ... vs Ramkumar Goyal on 5 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/160300308/
1 Rs.20,000/- to him.

sentences.text: Thereafter, the accused informed her that due to insufficiency of funds, an additional amount of Rs.1,100/- was required, which was also paid by the complainant.

The accused assured that the ATM would soon be installed and directed the complainant to complete the partition work, whereupon the complainant incurred an expenditure of Rs.40,000/- in constructing the partition in her shop.

Subsequently, after the partition had been completed, the accused advised the complainant to obtain a new cheque book from Canara Bank on the pretext that certain funds were to be deposited as bank security and informed her that he was travelling to Mumbai,
Maharashtra, and upon his return the ATM machine would be installed.
The complainant reposed trust in the accused.
The accused obtained three blank signed cheques from the complainant bearing cheque numbers 079576, 079577, and 079678 under the guise of completing bank formalities.

After some time, the complainant came to know that out of the three blank signed cheques so obtained, the accused had filled in two cheques for amounts of Rs.20,000/- and Rs.1,10,000/- respectively and had withdrawn a total sum of Rs.1,30,000/- from the complainant's bank account.

Upon being questioned, NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:7860 3 MCRC-406-2024 the accused stated that he had urgently required the money and had therefore withdrawn Rs.1,30,000/-, assuring that the same would be repaid shortly.

In acknowledgment of his liability and towards repayment of the said amount, the accused issued a cheque bearing No. 118728 dated 05.02.2014 for Rs.1,30,000/- drawn on his account with State Bank of India stating that upon presentation on 05 February 2014, the cheque would be duly honoured.
However, when the complainant presented the said cheque in her bank for encashment, the same was returned unpaid by the bank.
Thereafter, on 07.05.2014, the complainant, accompanied by her grandson Sonu and son-in- law Shankar Kotiya, visited the residence of the accused and demanded repayment of Rs.1,30,000/-.

The accused misbehaved with them, used abusive and filthy language, and threatened to kill the complainant if she came again to demand the money, further threatening to implicate her in false criminal cases.

The complainant lodged a written complaint regarding cheating and fraud against the accused at Police Station Jhansi Road and before the Superintendent of Police; however, as no action was taken, she filed a complaint before the Trial Court, which was registered under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code.
Upon the appearance of the accused, pre- charge evidence was recorded, and finding prima facie commission of an offence under Section 420 IPC, the matter was fixed for complainant's evidence.

During the course of trial, the accused filed an application dated 31.08.2021 under Section 91 of the Code of Criminal Procedure seeking direction to the complainant to produce the cheque bounce memorandum.

In reply, the complainant clarified that only the dishonoured cheque had been NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:7860 4 MCRC-406-2024 received from the bank and the memorandum was not in her possession.
The Trial Court rejected the said application.

Thereafter, the accused filed another application on 18.11.2022 seeking to bring on record a photocopy of the cheque return memo as a document, which was opposed by the complainant on 05.12.2022 on the ground that she had never provided any such memo to the accused.
The Trial Court rejected the said application on 18.12.2022.
Subsequently, the accused again filed an application under Section 91 CrPC seeking summoning of the cheque memorandum from State Bank of India, Jiwajiganj Branch, Lashkar, Gwalior.

The Trial Court allowed the said application and granted permission to summon the record from the bank; however,
the accused did not summon any record from the bank and instead filed another application under Section 65 of the Indian Evidence Act seeking permission to admit a photocopy of the memorandum dated 05.12.2014 as secondary evidence.

The complainant opposed the said application, contending Bhagwati Sahu W/O Shri Sundar Lal Sahu ... vs Ramkumar Goyal on 5 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/160300308/
2 that she had never supplied any copy of the bank memorandum to the accused and the document appeared to be fabricated and was being sought to be introduced fraudulently as secondary evidence.

sentences.text: Nevertheless, the Trial Court allowed the accused's application under Section 65 of the Evidence Act and permitted the photocopy of the memorandum dated 05.02.2014 to be admitted as secondary evidence.

Aggrieved by the order dated 19.10.2023 of the Trial Court, the complainant filed a criminal revision before the learned District and Sessions Judge, Gwalior, which was heard by the Eighth Additional Sessions Judge and dismissed the revision petition vide order dated 30.11.2023 as not maintainable, holding the impugned order to NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2026:MPHC-GWL:7860 5 MCRC-406-2024 be interlocutory in nature.
Being aggrieved by both the orders, the present petition has been filed.

3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that before the Trial Court, prior to filing the application under Section 65 of the Evidence Act, the accused had already moved two applications under Section 91 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and one application seeking to have the disputed document taken on record, all of which were rejected, wherein the complainant consistently objected on the ground that the photocopy of the document sought to be produced by the accused had never been supplied by the complainant to the accused and was forged; therefore,
despite such objection, the Trial Court's act of permitting the said document to be taken on record and allowing it to be admitted as secondary evidence without first conducting any inquiry into its genuineness is contrary to law.
4.

It is further submitted that although the application filed by the accused under Section 91 Cr.P.C.
was allowed by the Trial Court, the accused did not summon any record from the bank, and instead again filed an application under Section 65 of the Evidence Act seeking permission to exhibit the same disputed document as evidence, to which the complainant submitted a reply specifically contending that the disputed document was forged and a forged document cannot be admitted as secondary evidence unless and until its authenticity is duly verified.

The accused neither obtained certified copies of the return memos from the bank under the Right to Information Act nor summoned the bank record, and where the original document is admittedly within the knowledge of the accused as being NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:7860 6 MCRC-406-2024 preserved in the bank, an application under Section 65 of the Evidence Act ought not to have been allowed so as to admit secondary evidence; hence, the order of the Trial Court is liable to be set aside.

5. It is further submitted that when the Trial Court, by its order dated 18.12.2022, had rejected the accused's application to take the said document on record, the subsequent order dated 19.10.2023 permitting the same document to be taken on record is illegal and liable to be quashed, as the Trial Court does not possess the power of review.

The impugned order of the Trial Court permitting a forged document to be taken on record and admitted as secondary evidence materially affects the outcome of the case and has a direct bearing on the adjudication; therefore, the complainant preferred Criminal Revision Petition No. 433/2023 against the said order, which was erroneously dismissed by the Revisional Court as not maintainable, thereby committing a jurisdictional error,
and consequently the orders passed by both the Courts below are liable to be set aside.

sentences.text: Heard counsel for the petitioner and perused the record.

7. The principal question which arises for consideration is whether the order dated 19.10.2023 permitting the accused to lead secondary evidence by way of a photocopy of the alleged cheque return memorandum satisfies the requirements of Section 65 of the Evidence Act.
8. Section 65 of the Evidence Act permits secondary evidence of a document only in the contingencies enumerated therein.

It is well settled that before secondary evidence can be admitted,
the party seeking to rely upon it must lay a proper factual foundation establishing the existence and execution NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:7860 7 MCRC-406-2024 of the original document and the circumstances bringing the case within any of the clauses of Section 65.
Mere production of a photocopy does not ipso facto entitle a party to have the same admitted as secondary evidence.
The Court is required to be satisfied regarding the existence of the original document and the reasons for its non-production.
9. In the present case, the record reflects that the accused had knowledge that the original cheque return memorandum, if any, would be in the custody of the concerned bank.

An application under Section 91 Cr.P.C. seeking summoning of the record from the bank was allowed by the Trial Court;
however, the accused did not take steps to summon the record.
Without exhausting that remedy, he sought to introduce a photocopy of the alleged memorandum as secondary evidence.
No material was placed on record to demonstrate that the original was lost, destroyed, or otherwise unavailable despite due diligence.
There is also nothing on record to indicate that the bank declined to furnish certified copies.
In absence of such foundational facts, the essential preconditions for invoking Section 65 were not satisfied.
10. Furthermore, the petitioner had specifically raised an objection that the photocopy sought to be introduced was forged and fabricated.

In such circumstances, the Trial Court was under an obligation to examine whether the document sought to be admitted as secondary evidence had been duly proved to exist and whether the requirements of law were fulfilled.
The impugned order dated 19.10.2023 does not disclose any consideration of these aspects and mechanically allows the application.
NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-GWL:7860 8 MCRC-406-2024 11.
It is also noteworthy that the Trial Court had earlier rejected an application seeking to take the same document on record.

Though a criminal court does possess the power to recall or reconsider interlocutory orders in appropriate cases to secure the ends of justice, such power cannot be exercised in a manner that circumvents statutory requirements or without recording reasons demonstrating change of circumstances or discovery of new material.
The impugned order does not reflect any such justification.
12. This Court, in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C., is empowered to prevent abuse of the process of the Court and to secure the ends of justice.
When an order is passed in disregard of statutory requirements and results in manifest injustice, interference is warranted.

sentences.text: In view of the aforesaid analysis, the order dated 19.10.2023 passed by the learned Trial Court allowing the application under Section 65 of the Evidence Act and permitting the photocopy of the cheque return memorandum dated 05.02.2014 to be admitted as secondary evidence is unsustainable in law and is hereby set aside.
Consequently, the order dated 30.11.2023 passed by the learned 8th Additional Sessions Judge, Gwalior in Criminal Revision No. 433/2023 is also set aside.
14. The petition stands allowed in the aforesaid terms.
